newsitem.title: SPAIN: Madrid airport struggles with backlog and strike.
newsitem.headline: Madrid airport struggles with backlog and strike.

text.p: Madrid's Barajas airport, forced to shut down completely for the first time in its history on Tuesday night, on Wednesday braced for possible strike disruption, airport officials said.

Tuesday's closure, caused by a failure of the runway lighting systems after a fire in electrical cables earlier in the day, lasted five hours and affected some 300 flights which had to be cancelled or diverted.

"We've known for some time that we needed to extend Barajas," the airport's director Jose Serrano told Spanish National Radio on Wednesday. "If we'd had a third runway yesterday we would not have faced this problem."
The contract to build a third runway was awarded at the end of November and construction will take almost two years.
Airlines which had diverted flights on Tuesday night would have to make a special effort to reposition their aircraft for flights on Wednesday, Serrano added.
On Wednesday Barajas along with other Spanish airports faced possible complications from a nationwide civil servants strike called to protest against next year's wage freeze.
The government has decreed a minimum staffing level of 80 percent for air traffic controllers and other safety workers to ensure near normal functioning of the airport.
Spanish radio said at first light that these minimum levels were being respected at Barajas.

Iberia said at 0915 GMT that it had cancelled 14 flights, mainly short haul services, because crew or aircraft were in the wrong place after Tuesday's closure, and that some intercontinental flights were leaving or arriving late but that the strike was apparently not causing further problems.
Air Europa said on Tuesday it was prepared for some disruption to flights.
Among passengers who had to change their travel plans on Tuesday was Spain's Queen Sofia who cancelled a trip to Paraguay.
